## Statement

Let $g\in C^7(J,\mathbb R)$ on an open interval $J$, and let $x_0\in J$ satisfy $g'(x_0)=0$ and $g''(x_0)\ne0$. Then some open interval $J_0\subset J$ about $x_0$ admits a $C^5$ increasing diffeomorphism $\Phi:J_0\to\Phi(J_0)$ such that
$$g(x)=g(x_0)+\frac{\sigma}{2}\Phi(x)^2,\qquad \Phi(x_0)=0,\qquad \Phi'(x_0)=\sqrt{|g''(x_0)|},\qquad \sigma=\operatorname{sgn}(g''(x_0)).$$

1.1 Twice applying [F1] to $g'$ and $g$ gives, for $x$ near $x_0$, $g(x)-g(x_0)=(x-x_0)^2\int_0^1(1-t)g''(x_0+t(x-x_0))\,dt.$ Set $q(x)=2\int_0^1(1-t)g''(x_0+t(x-x_0))\,dt$. Repeated differentiation under this compact parameter integral gives $q^{(j)}(x)=2\int_0^1(1-t)t^jg^{(j+2)}(x_0+t(x-x_0))\,dt$ for $0\le j\le5$: each difference quotient converges uniformly in $t$ by the mean-value theorem and uniform continuity of the next derivative on a compact neighborhood. Thus $q\in C^5$ and $q(x_0)=g''(x_0)$. [given, F1, F3, construct]
cases.evidence: The positive square root of the integral remainder fixes the coordinate, and a positive derivative fixes its inverse uniquely.

## Definition

Let $A\in\mathbb F^{n\times n}$ be Hermitian positive semidefinite with $n\ge1$, let $S\in\mathbb F^{n\times s}$ with $s\ge0$ be any finite sketch matrix, and put $W=S^*AS\in\mathbb F^{s\times s}$. The **Nyström approximation** associated with $(A,S)$ is
$\widehat A_{\mathrm{nys}}=AS\,W^\dagger S^*A$.

The Moore-Penrose inverse is defined for every finite matrix, including singular $W$, and is unique by the dependencies. No rank, sampling, or probabilistic condition is part of this definition.

## Statement

Let $P=LL^T$ with $L\in\mathbb R^{d\times r}$ and let
$Q=L_Q L_Q^T$ with $L_Q\in\mathbb R^{n\times s}$, where zero columns and
rank deficiency are allowed. For any real $F\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$,
form $G=[FL\;L_Q]$ and append zero columns if needed so that the transpose
has at least $n$ rows. In exact arithmetic, if $G^T=UR$ is a reduced QR
factorization with $U^TU=I$, then $L^-:=R^T$ satisfies
$$
L^-(L^-)^T=FPF^T+Q.
$$

1.1 The padded zero columns do not change the Gram matrix, so $$GG^T=[FL\;L_Q][FL\;L_Q]^T=FLL^TF^T+L_QL_Q^T=FPF^T+Q.$$ The cross terms are absent because the two factors occupy disjoint column blocks. [given, algebra]
cases.evidence: Zero columns and rank deficiency are explicitly admitted, and an empty column block contributes a zero Gram matrix.

## Definition

Let $m\ge1$, let $G\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let
$f:G\to\mathbb R^m$ be $C^3$ ([[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]];
the $C^3$ convention is that of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]).
The one-dimensional conservation system with state domain $G$ is
$$u_t+\partial_x f(u)=0,\qquad u(t,x)\in G,$$
where $u$ is the conserved state and $f$ its flux. Its flux Jacobian is
$A(u)=Df(u)$. The system is **strictly hyperbolic on an open set $N\subseteq G$**
if, for every $u\in N$, $A(u)$ has $m$ distinct real eigenvalues, written in
increasing order $\lambda_1(u)<\cdots<\lambda_m(u)$. An **$i$th characteristic
family** on $N$ is a $C^2$ right-eigenvector field $r_i:N\to\mathbb R^m\setminus\{0\}$
with $A(u)r_i(u)=\lambda_i(u)r_i(u)$. It is **genuinely nonlinear** on $N$ if
$D\lambda_i(u)r_i(u)$ is nowhere zero there; after shrinking $N$ its sign is
constant. It is **linearly degenerate** on $N$ if $D\lambda_i(u)r_i(u)=0$
throughout $N$. Rescaling $r_i$ by a nonzero constant changes the wave-strength
parameter but not the family.

For $Q=(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$, a locally bounded map $u:Q\to G$ is a
**distributional weak solution with initial data $u_0$** if
$$\int_Q\bigl(u\cdot\varphi_t+f(u)\cdot\varphi_x\bigr)\,dt\,dx=0$$
for every vector test function $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(Q;\mathbb R^m)$ and
$u(t,\cdot)\to u_0$ in $L^1_{\rm loc}(\mathbb R;\mathbb R^m)$ as
$t\downarrow0$. A **Riemann initial datum** is the step
$u_0(x)=u_L$ for $x<0$ and $u_0(x)=u_R$ for $x>0$.
cases.evidence: The eigenvector field is supplied as part of a characteristic family; sorting distinct real eigenvalues is canonical.

## Definition

Let $h>0$, let $I_i=[ih,(i+1)h)$, let $x_i=(i+\tfrac12)h$ be its center, and write $x_{i+1/2}=(i+1)h$ and $x_{i-1/2}=ih$ for its right and left faces. A **cell average** of a locally integrable scalar function $u$ is $U_i=h^{-1}\int_{I_i}u(x)\,dx$. The cells are half-open only to form a partition; the choice of endpoint representatives does not change an integral.

Here **MUSCL/minmod** means the piecewise-linear reconstruction with the limiter defined next; **nodal ENO2** means the two-stencil quadratic selector defined below; and **cell-average WENO5-JS/WENO-Z** means the three-candidate reconstructions with the normalized nonlinear weights displayed below. These names specify the constructions and do not, by themselves, assert an accuracy or stability property.

For real $a,b$, define
$$\operatorname{minmod}(a,b)=\begin{cases}\operatorname{sgn}(a)\min(|a|,|b|),&ab>0,\\0,&ab\le0.\end{cases}$$
The **MUSCL/minmod reconstruction** assigns the cell slope $s_i=h^{-1}\operatorname{minmod}(U_i-U_{i-1},U_{i+1}-U_i)$ and the two face states $U_{i-1/2}^{+,M}=U_i-hs_i/2$ and $U_{i+1/2}^{-,M}=U_i+hs_i/2$. Here $+$ denotes a trace from the right cell and $-$ a trace from the left cell.

For separate **nodal** data $V_j=u(y_j)$ at $y_j=jh$, define the second divided difference by $[y_a,y_b,y_c]V=(((V_c-V_b)/(y_c-y_b))-((V_b-V_a)/(y_b-y_a)))/(y_c-y_a)$. ## Statement

For $m>1$ and $C>0$, put
$$\beta=\frac1{m+1},\qquad k=\frac{m-1}{2m(m+1)},\qquad u(t,x)=t^{-\beta} \left(C-kx^2t^{-2\beta}\right)_+^{1/(m-1)} \quad(t>0,\ x\in\mathbb R),$$
where $r_+=\max(r,0)$. Then $u$ is a nonnegative distributional solution
of the one-dimensional porous-medium equation
$u_t=(u^m)_{xx}$ on $(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$. For every $t>0$ it is
supported in
$$|x|\le\sqrt{C/k}\,t^{1/(m+1)},$$
so its support radius is finite and grows like $t^{1/(m+1)}$.

1.1 Write $\alpha=1/(m-1)$, $y=xt^{-\beta}$, and $F(y)=(C-ky^2)_+^\alpha$. Then $u=t^{-\beta}F(y)$ and $u^m=t^{-m\beta}G(y)$, where $G(y)=(C-ky^2)_+^{\alpha+1}$. Inside the positivity set, $$u_t=t^{-\beta-1}(-\beta F-\beta yF'),\qquad (u^m)_{xx}=t^{-(m+2)\beta}G''.$$ Equality of the time powers requires $\beta+1=(m+2)\beta$, giving $\beta=1/(m+1)$. [A1, given, algebra]

Likewise, $u_t$ has only a locally integrable $q^{\alpha-1}$ singularity; the moving interface contributes no time delta because the jump of $u$ across it is zero. Hence the pointwise identity of step 2.1 extends distributionally across the interface. [A1, step 2.1, algebra]

## Definition

Fix an integer $N\ge1$, put $h=1/N$, and let $x_j=jh$ for $j=0,\ldots,N$. The cells are $K_j=[x_{j-1},x_j]$. For $g_0,g_1\in\mathbb R$, let $S_h(g_0,g_1)$ be the finite-dimensional space of continuous functions on $[0,1]$ that are affine on each cell and have endpoint values $g_0,g_1$. Write $V_h=S_h(0,0)$ for the homogeneous test and trial space. “P1” means polynomial degree at most one on each interval.

Let $\epsilon>0$, $b\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$, and $f\in C([0,1])$. The stationary boundary-value problem is to find $u\in C^2([0,1])$ such that $-\epsilon u''+b u'=f$ on $(0,1)$, with prescribed endpoint values $u(0)=g_0$ and $u(1)=g_1$. Its dimensionless cell Péclet number is $\mathrm{Pe}=|b|h/(2\epsilon)>0$. The stability theorem on this page uses the homogeneous branch $g_0=g_1=0$; the general endpoint notation also permits the boundary-layer example.
cases.reason: There is at least one positive-length cell; the given endpoints form a nonempty interval.

## Definition

For $x\ne y$ in $\mathbb R^2$, the logarithmic Laplace fundamental solution is $G_2(x,y)=-(2\pi)^{-1}\log|x-y|$. If $\Gamma$ is a closed piecewise-smooth curve and $\lambda$ is a smooth density, its two-dimensional single-layer trace is
$$V_\Gamma\lambda(x)=-\frac1{2\pi}\int_\Gamma\log|x-y|\lambda(y)\,ds_y.$$

For a compact set $K\subset\mathbb R^2$ with positive finite logarithmic capacity, let $\mathcal P(K)$ be the Borel probability measures supported on $K$, let $I(\mu)=\int_K\int_K\log\frac1{|x-y|}\,d\mu(x)\,d\mu(y)$ with value $+\infty$ on the diagonal, and define
$$I(K)=\inf_{\mu\in\mathcal P(K)} I(\mu),\qquad \operatorname{cap}(K)=e^{-I(K)}.$$
This definition fixes length units: scaling $K$ changes its capacity and adds a constant-mode term to the logarithmic layer operator, as proved separately by the homothety theorem on this page.

## Definition

Let $k>0$, $x\in\mathbb R$ be the Cartesian normal coordinate, and $y\in\mathbb R^2$ the tangential coordinate. Let $\sigma$ be nonnegative, continuous, piecewise $C^1$, and zero for $x\le0$. Define
$$S(x)=\int_0^x\sigma(t)\,dt,\qquad X(x)=x+iS(x),\qquad s(x)=X'(x)=1+i\sigma(x).$$
The pulled-back constant-coefficient Helmholtz operator in the layer is
$$\frac1{s(x)}\partial_x\left(\frac1{s(x)}\partial_x\right)+\Delta_y+k^2.$$
This definition concerns the homogeneous Cartesian branch only; it makes no claim for heterogeneous media, curved stretches, grazing or evanescent uniform attenuation, discretizations, or finite-element convergence.

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^2$ be a bounded open polygonal domain with finitely many straight sides and corner set $\mathcal C=\{c_1,\ldots,c_m\}$, with interior angle at each corner strictly between $0$ and $2\pi$. Let $0\le\beta_i<1$ and write $\Phi_\gamma(x)=\prod_{i=1}^m|x-c_i|^{\gamma_i}$ for a vector $\gamma\in[0,\infty)^m$. For integer $k\ge2$, define

$$
\|v\|_{H^{k,2}_\beta(\Omega)}^2=\|v\|_{H^1(\Omega)}^2+\sum_{j=2}^k\sum_{|\alpha|=j}\|\Phi_{\beta+j-2}D^\alpha v\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2,
$$

where $(\beta+j-2)_i=\beta_i+j-2$ and a zero exponent contributes the factor one. Let $u\in H^{k,2}_\beta(\Omega)$ for every integer $k\ge2$, with real-valued weak derivatives, and suppose constants $C_u,d_u>0$ satisfy

$$
\left\|\Phi_{\beta+j-2}\sum_{|\alpha|=j}|D^\alpha u|\right\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\le C_ud_u^{j-2}(j-2)!\qquad(j\ge2).
$$

For each fixed $0<a<\min_i(1-\beta_i)$ there are constants $C,A,R>0$ such that the weak class of $u$ has a unique representative $\widetilde u\in C(\overline\Omega)$, smooth up to every open side away from corners, and for $0<r=|x-c_i|<R$,

$$
|\widetilde u(x)-\widetilde u(c_i)|\le Cr^a,\qquad |D^\alpha\widetilde u(x)|\le CA^{|\alpha|}|\alpha|!r^{a-|\alpha|}\quad(|\alpha|\ge1).
$$

On every compact subset of $\overline\Omega\setminus\mathcal C$, the derivatives satisfy ordinary factorial bounds $|D^\alpha u|\le C_0A_0^{|\alpha|}|\alpha|!$. On every shape-regular affine triangle $K\subset\Omega$ whose closure avoids $\mathcal C$ and whose ratio $h_K/\operatorname{dist}(K,\mathcal C)$ is bounded above and below by fixed positive constants, where $\operatorname{dist}(K,\mathcal C)=\inf_{x\in K,c\in\mathcal C}|x-c|$, set $r_K=\min(R,\operatorname{dist}(K,\mathcal C))$. After subtracting a suitable constant from the pullback $\widehat u$ to the reference triangle of [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]], $\|D^\alpha\widehat u\|_\infty\le C A_1^{|\alpha|}|\alpha|!r_K^a$ for every multi-index $\alpha$, with constants uniform over this family. If a shape-regular triangle $K\subset\Omega$ of diameter $h<R$ has a corner $c_i$ as a vertex, its vertex affine interpolant $a_K$ satisfies

$$
|u-a_K|_{H^1(K)}\le Ch^a,\qquad \|u-a_K\|_{L^2(K)}\le Ch^{a+1}.
$$

1.1 On the unit square, for smooth $v$ the one-dimensional identity $|g(t)|\le\int_0^1|g(s)|ds+\int_0^1|g'(s)|ds$ applied first in $x$ and then in $y$ gives $\|v\|_\infty\le\|v\|_{L^1}+\|v_x\|_{L^1}+\|v_y\|_{L^1}+\|v_{xy}\|_{L^1}\le\sum_{i,j=0}^1\|\partial_x^i\partial_y^jv\|_{L^2}$ by [F2]. For $v\in H^2((0,1)^2)$ extend across $x=0$ by $Ev(x,y)=3v(-x,y)-2v(-2x,y)$ for small $x<0$, and across $x=1$ by $Ev(x,y)=3v(2-x,y)-2v(3-2x,y)$ for small $x>1$; use the same two formulas in $y$. The coefficients satisfy $3-2=1$ for values and $-3+4=1$ for first normal derivatives. For a smooth test $\phi$ across $x=0$, changing variables in the zeroth-order pairing gives $\psi_0(t)=\phi(t)-3\phi(-t)+2\phi(-t/2)$, so $\psi_0(0)=0$. For the first normal derivative, the corresponding test combination is $\psi_1(t)=\phi(t)+3\phi(-t)-4\phi(-t/2)$, also with $\psi_1(0)=0$. These formulas follow by rewriting the reflected integrals over $t>0$ and applying the chain rule. Multiply each combined test by a cutoff that is zero on $(0,\varepsilon)$ and one on $(2\varepsilon,\infty)$ before using the weak derivative identity on the original open square. If $|\chi_\varepsilon\prime|\le C/\varepsilon$, then $|\psi_j\chi_\varepsilon\prime|\le C$ on the strip because $\psi_j(t)=O(t)$; for any relevant $g\in L^2$, Cauchy--Schwarz bounds the cutoff error by $C\sqrt{2\varepsilon}\|g\|_{L^2(0,2\varepsilon)}\le C\sqrt{2\varepsilon}\|g\|_{L^2(0,1)}\to0$. Thus the reflected piecewise formulas are the weak derivatives through order two, including mixed derivatives. Changes of variables bound each derivative norm by a fixed multiple of $\|v\|_{H^2}$. Reflect successively across the four sides, cut off in the enlarged square, and mollify. For every weak derivative through order two, inserting a translated compactly supported kernel into its weak derivative identity gives $D^\alpha(v*\varphi_\varepsilon)=(D^\alpha v)*\varphi_\varepsilon$ on the original square: the sign from integration by parts cancels the sign from differentiating the kernel in its integration variable. Thus [F3] gives smooth approximants converging in $H^2$. The smooth inequality makes them uniformly Cauchy, yielding a continuous representative and the same bound for every $H^2$ class. Scaling gives $\|v\|_{L^\infty(Q)}\le C(r^{-1}\|v\|_2+\|Dv\|_2+r\|D^2v\|_2)$ on a rectangle of side comparable to $r$; a parallelogram with fixed aspect ratio has the same estimate after an affine change of variables. [A1, F1, F2, F3, given, construct]

## Statement

Let $J=[a,b]$ be a compact bracket, let $y$ be an exact incoming characteristic on $J$, and let $g(t,x)$ be a boundary guard that is $L_g$-Lipschitz in its state argument on a tube containing the exact path and a dense reconstruction $U$. Suppose $h(t):=g(t,y(t))$ has a root $\tau\in J$ and a declared orientation $\sigma\in\{-1,1\}$ with $\sigma h'(t)\ge\nu>0$ throughout $J$. If
$$\sup_{t\in J}\|y(t)-U(t)\|_2\le\eta,\qquad |g(\widehat\tau,U(\widehat\tau))|\le\varepsilon,\qquad \widehat\tau\in J,$$
then the matched first-hit time satisfies
$$|\widehat\tau-\tau|\le\Delta:=\frac{L_g\eta+\varepsilon}{\nu}.$$
If the boundary value $\beta(t,x)$ is Lipschitz in time and state with constants $L_t^\beta,L_x^\beta$ on the same tube and $\|y'(t)\|_2\le M$, then
$$|\beta(\widehat\tau,U(\widehat\tau))-\beta(\tau,y(\tau))|\le L_t^\beta\Delta+L_x^\beta(\eta+M\Delta).$$
This is a local one-hit bound. It gives no conclusion at grazing, unresolved, or simultaneous events.

1.1 By [F2], the transversality hypothesis is the mode derivative condition required by [F3]. Apply [F3] to this matched bracket with the stated $\eta,\varepsilon,L_g,\nu$; it yields the unique transverse root and the displayed bound $|\widehat\tau-\tau|\le\Delta$. [given, F1, F2, F3]

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $f$ be finite and locally semiconvex near $0\in\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge1$: on some Euclidean ball ([[def-metric-ball]]), $f(x)+\lambda|x|^2/2$ is convex ([[def-convex-and-strictly-convex-functions-on-euclidean-sets]]) for a finite $\lambda\ge0$. Suppose $0$ is a strict local maximum of $f$. ## Statement

For a finite index set $E$ and arrays $x,y\in\mathbb C^E$, the Euclidean norm of [[def-nufft-finite-array-norms]] satisfies
$$\|x+y\|_2\le\|x\|_2+\|y\|_2.$$

1.1 First prove Cauchy–Schwarz for these arrays. If $y=0$, its inner product with $x$ is zero. If $y\ne0$, choose $e_0$ with $y_{e_0}\ne0$; [F2]–[F3] give $\|y\|_2^2=\sum_e|y_e|^2>0$. Put $a=\langle x,y\rangle_E$ and $c=a/\|y\|_2^2$. Expanding the finite sum using [F1] and conjugation laws gives $0\le\|x-cy\|_2^2=\|x\|_2^2-\frac{|a|^2}{\|y\|_2^2}.$ Multiplying by the positive denominator yields $|\langle x,y\rangle_E|^2\le\|x\|_2^2\|y\|_2^2$; all quantities are nonnegative, so [F4] gives $|\langle x,y\rangle_E|\le\|x\|_2\|y\|_2$. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, choose, algebra]

## Definition

For $A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, $n\ge1$, let $Z=Z_n$ be the lower shift with $Z_{i+1,i}=1$ for $0\le i<n-1$ and all other entries zero. Its lower-shift (Stein) displacement is
$$\nabla_Z(A):=A-ZAZ^*.$$
The **displacement rank** of $A$ with respect to this fixed shift is $\operatorname{rank}(\nabla_Z(A))$. A pair of matrices $G,H\in\mathbb C^{n\times r}$ is a **generator of width $r$** when
$$\nabla_Z(A)=GH^*.$$
Such a factorization is a representation of the displacement, not a factorization of $A$ itself. A matrix with displacement rank at most $r$ is called Toeplitz-like (relative to this shift). This definition makes no conditioning, pivot-growth, or numerical-stability assertion.
cases.evidence: The shift is fixed by the index order, and a supplied pair of finite generators requires no arbitrary selection.

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice for the finite-dimensional Gaussian probability law.
Let $N\ge1$ be an integer, and let $(X_i)_{i=1}^N$ and $(Y_i)_{i=1}^N$ be
finite centered real Gaussian families. If $\mathbb E(X_i-X_j)^2\le\mathbb E(Y_i-Y_j)^2$ for every
$i,j$, then $\mathbb E\max_iX_i\le\mathbb E\max_iY_i$.
Here a finite centered real Gaussian family means a finite real vector that
is a real-linear image of finitely many independent standard real Gaussian
scalars.

1.1 Take independent copies of $X,Y$, with covariance entries $(C_X)_{ij}=\mathbb E(X_iX_j)$ and $(C_Y)_{ij}=\mathbb E(Y_iY_j)$, and represent them as independent linear images of standard Gaussian coordinates using [A1]. For $0<t<1$ put $Z(t)=\sqrt tY+\sqrt{1-t}X$ and $F_\beta(z)=\beta^{-1}\log\sum_{i=1}^Ne^{\beta z_i}$ with $w_i=e^{\beta z_i}/\sum_je^{\beta z_j}$. The soft maximum has at most linear growth, so its Gaussian slice is integrable. On each compact subinterval of $(0,1)$, $|\partial_tF_\beta(Z(t))|\le\|\nabla F_\beta\|_2(\|Y\|_2/(2\sqrt t)+\|X\|_2/(2\sqrt{1-t}))$ has an integrable uniform bound, so [F3] passes the derivative under the finite Gaussian integral. For the coordinate integration by parts, fix all coordinates but $r=g_j$, and let $\varphi(r)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-r^2/2}$. The functions to which it is applied are first derivatives of $F_\beta$ composed with linear maps; they and their $r$ derivatives are smooth and bounded for fixed $\beta$. On $[-R,R]$, [F5] with $u=f$ and $v=\varphi$ gives $\int_{-R}^R r f(r)\varphi(r)\,dr=\int_{-R}^R f'(r)\varphi(r)\,dr-[f(r)\varphi(r)]_{-R}^R$. The boundary term tends to zero since $f$ is bounded and $\varphi(\pm R)\to0$. The integrands are dominated by constant multiples of $|r|\varphi(r)$ and $\varphi(r)$, respectively, so [F4] takes $R\to\infty$. Both majorants are integrable. Their bounds are uniform in the other coordinates, and [F6] integrates the resulting identity over those coordinates. Applying this coordinatewise to a linear image $W=L g$ gives $\mathbb E[W_i f(W)]=\sum_j\operatorname{Cov}(W_i,W_j)\mathbb E[\partial_jf(W)]$, including singular covariance matrices. Apply it separately to $X,Y$ in the derivative to obtain $\frac{d}{dt}\mathbb EF_\beta(Z(t))=\frac12\sum_{i,j}(C_Y-C_X)_{ij}\mathbb E[\partial_{ij}F_\beta(Z(t))]$. Since $\partial_{ij}F_\beta=\beta(w_i\mathbf1_{i=j}-w_iw_j)$, symmetry rewrites this as $\frac\beta4\mathbb E\sum_{i,j}w_iw_j(\mathbb E(Y_i-Y_j)^2-\mathbb E(X_i-X_j)^2)\ge0$ by the assumed increment order. [given, A1, A2, F3, F4, F5, F6, algebra]
cases.reason: Increment-variance domination implies an expected-maximum inequality through Gaussian interpolation.

## Statement

Let $A\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$ over $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, with $m\ge n\ge1$, and let $0\le k\le n$, $f\ge1$. The spectral norm is $\|M\|_2=\sup_{\|x\|_2=1}\|Mx\|_2$, and $\sigma_j(M)$ is the $j$th singular value in decreasing order. The procedure [[alg-strong-rrqr-interpolative-decomposition]] returns the exact zero approximation for $k=0$ and the exact reconstruction for $k=n$. For $1\le k<n$, assume $\operatorname{rank}(A)=n$ and its exact-arithmetic strong-RRQR call returns success, and write $g=(1+f^2k(n-k))^{1/2}$ for the returned blocks. Then $T(:,J)=I_k$, $\max_{i,j}|T_{ij}|\le f$, and

$$\|A-A(:,J)T\|_2=\|R_{22}\|_2\le g\,\sigma_{k+1}(A).$$

No decomposition or error conclusion is asserted when the procedure returns a rank-loss or budget status. This theorem gives no finite-precision error bound for a returned candidate; such a bound requires verified score bounds and a reconstruction certificate for the actual returned interpolative decomposition.

1.1 If $k=0$, the algorithm returns $T$ with zero rows, so $A(:,J)T=0$ and the residual is $A$. If $k=n$, it returns $J=(1,\ldots,n)$ and $T=I_n$, so the residual is zero. Assume henceforth $1\le k<n$ and exact-arithmetic success. [given, F1, algebra]

## Definition

Let $P(\lambda)=\sum_{j=0}^{m}A_j\lambda^j$ be regular of grade $m$, let $[\alpha:\beta]$ be a projective parameter, let $x\in\mathbb C^n\setminus\{0\}$, and choose positive weights $\omega_0,\ldots,\omega_m$. Write $r:=P_h(\alpha,\beta)x$. The **coefficientwise weighted Frobenius backward error** is the infimum
$$\eta_F(P,[\alpha:\beta],x;\omega):=\inf\left\{\left(\sum_{j=0}^{m}\frac{\|\Delta A_j\|_F^2}{\omega_j^2}\right)^{1/2}:\ \sum_{j=0}^{m}(A_j+\Delta A_j)\alpha^j\beta^{m-j}x=0,\quad \Delta A_j\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}\right\}.$$
The perturbations of distinct coefficients are unrestricted and measured in the displayed weighted product norm; no symmetry or other coefficient structure is imposed. Replacing $(\alpha,\beta)$ by $(c\alpha,c\beta)$ for $c\ne0$ multiplies the constraint by $c^m$ and leaves its zero set unchanged, so the infimum depends only on $[\alpha:\beta]$. The infimum is defined for finite and infinite projective parameters. The next theorem proves that it is attained and gives its exact value.
cases.reason: The polynomial coefficient tuple always contains the constant coefficient, and the supplied eigenvector is explicitly nonzero.

## Statement

Let $M\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ be Schur stable and let $r$ satisfy $\rho(M)<r<1$. For the Euclidean induced operator norm there is a finite $C_r$ such that
$$\|M^k\|_2\le C_r r^k\qquad(k\ge0).$$
For a real matrix, interpret the same statement on its complexification.

1.1 If $n=0$, the unique endomorphism and every power of it is the zero map on the zero domain; its operator norm is zero, so the assertion holds with $C_r=0$. Assume now $n\ge1$ and regard a real matrix, if present, as a complex matrix. Its characteristic polynomial is a nonconstant complex polynomial, so [F5] and [F2] give $M=UTU^*$ with $U$ unitary and $T=D+N$, where $D$ is diagonal and $N$ is strictly upper triangular. Similar matrices have the same eigenvalues: $Mv=\lambda v$ is equivalent to $T(U^*v)=\lambda(U^*v)$. By [F7] and [F8], the eigenvalues are the diagonal entries of $T$; hence $\rho(M)=\max_i|T_{ii}|=\|D\|_2$, where the last equality follows directly from the Euclidean induced norm. Set $\rho=\rho(M)<r$. Each occurrence of $N$ in a product raises the row-to-column index, while $D$ preserves it, so every word containing at least $n$ copies of $N$ is zero. [A1, F1, F2, F5, F7, F8, construct]
cases.evidence: The proof explicitly treats the zero-dimensional endomorphism with zero operator norm and a zero prefactor.

## Statement

For $m\in\mathbb N_0$, $T\ge0$, and integer $N\ge1$, let $h=1/N$, $t_j=(j-\tfrac12)h$ for $1\le j\le N$, and
$$Q_{m,N}(T)=h\sum_{j=1}^N t_j^{2m}e^{-Tt_j^2}.$$
Then all quadrature weights and summands are positive and
$$|F_m(T)-Q_{m,N}(T)|\le\frac{m+T}{2N}.$$
Consequently, for $0\le T\le T_{\max}$, the same positive rule has the uniform enclosure error $(m+T_{\max})/(2N)$.

1.1 For $m=0$, $f'(t)=-2Tt e^{-Tt^2}$, so $|f'(t)|\le2T$. For $m\ge1$, differentiation gives $f'(t)=2m t^{2m-1}e^{-Tt^2}-2Tt^{2m+1}e^{-Tt^2}$; since $0\le t\le1$ and $e^{-Tt^2}\le1$, $|f'(t)|\le2m+2T$. Thus the Lipschitz constant $L=2m+2T$ is valid in both cases by [F2]. [given, F1, F2, algebra, L9]

## Statement

Let $\Gamma$ and the chartwise norm on $H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$ be as in [[def-bem-lipschitz-polyhedral-boundary-and-trace-spaces]]. For a measurable $g$ define
$$\|g\|_{H^{1/2}_{\mathrm{ch}}(\Gamma)}^2=\|g\|_{L^2(\Gamma)}^2+\int_\Gamma\int_\Gamma\frac{|g(x)-g(y)|^2}{|x-y|^3}\,ds_xds_y.$$
There are constants $c,C>0$ depending only on the fixed finite atlas and partition such that, first for smooth $g$ and then by completion,
$$c\|g\|_{H^{1/2}(\Gamma)}\le\|g\|_{H^{1/2}_{\mathrm{ch}}(\Gamma)}\le C\|g\|_{H^{1/2}(\Gamma)}.$$

2.1 Write $g_j=\chi_jg$, so $g=\sum_{j=1}^Jg_j$. The inequality $|g(x)-g(y)|^2\le J\sum_j|g_j(x)-g_j(y)|^2$ shows that the global chordal norm is bounded by the sum of localized chordal norms from step 1.1. Conversely, $|g_j(x)-g_j(y)|\le |\chi_j(x)|\,|g(x)-g(y)|+|g(y)|\,|\chi_j(x)-\chi_j(y)|.$ Each $\chi_j$ is Lipschitz. The second term contributes at most $C\|g\|_{L^2}^2$ to the squared seminorm, since $\int_\Gamma|x-y|^{-1}ds_x$ is uniformly bounded in $y$: in each chart the surface area of a radius-$r$ disk is at most $Cr^2$, and summing dyadic annuli gives $\int_{|x-y|<1}|x-y|^{-1}ds_x\le C\sum_{m\ge0}2^{-m}<\infty$; the part $|x-y|\ge1$ is bounded by the finite surface area. Hence the sum of localized chordal norms is bounded by the global chordal norm. Combining both comparisons with step 1.1 proves the two-sided equivalence for smooth $g$. Equivalent norms have the same completion, which proves the stated extension. [A1, F1, step 1.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. On a finite matching affine simplicial mesh or a finite face-to-face affine tensor-box mesh, a piecewise polynomial scalar function whose two traces agree on every interior facet belongs to $H^1(\Omega)$, and its weak gradient equals its ordinary cellwise polynomial gradient almost everywhere. The simplex degrees may vary by cell; the box degrees may also vary.

1.2 Suppose the cells are affine tensor boxes. Fix a coordinate $i$. On each cell, apply [F3] to the smooth field $v\varphi e_i$; its divergence is $v\,\partial_i\varphi+g_i\varphi$. Sum the finitely many resulting identities. At an interior face the two outward normals are opposite, because the adjacent cell interiors lie on opposite sides of its supporting hyperplane; the common trace in [F1] therefore makes the two fluxes cancel. The boundary-face terms vanish since $\varphi$ has compact support in $\Omega$. Thus $\int_\Omega v\,\partial_i\varphi=-\int_\Omega g_i\varphi$. [F1, F3, given, algebra]
cases.evidence: The zero polynomial has matching traces and zero cellwise weak gradient.

## Statement

For every policy $\pi$ in [[def-na-finite-state-discounted-bellman-system]],
the matrix $A^\pi=cI-Q^\pi$ is nonsingular, $(A^\pi)^{-1}$ is entrywise
nonnegative, and each diagonal entry of $(A^\pi)^{-1}$ is strictly positive.

1.1 Nonsingularity. Suppose $Az=0$ for a nonzero real vector $z$. The finite set $\{|z_j|:1\le j\le n\}$ has a maximum by [F3]; choose an index $i$ attaining it, so $|z_i|=\max_j|z_j|>0$. By the zero row sum, $(Az)_i=cz_i+\sum_{j\ne i}q_{ij}(z_i-z_j)$. If $z_i>0$, every term in the sum is nonnegative and $cz_i>0$, contradicting $(Az)_i=0$. If $z_i<0$, every sum term is nonpositive and $cz_i<0$, again a contradiction. Thus the kernel is zero, and [F2] makes the square matrix nonsingular. [F1, F2, F3, choose, algebra]
cases.reason: The policy system has a positive finite state count; the extremal-coordinate argument starts from a nonzero vector.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, and let $u:U\to\mathbb R$ be locally semiconvex: around each point there is a Euclidean ball ([[def-metric-ball]]) and $c\ge0$ such that $x\mapsto u(x)+c|x|^2/2$ is convex in the sense of [[def-convex-and-strictly-convex-functions-on-euclidean-sets]]. Outside a set null in the cube-cover sense of [[def-null-and-content-zero-in-rn]], there are $p\in\mathbb R^n$ and a symmetric matrix $A$ with
$$u(x+h)=u(x)+p\cdot h+\tfrac12h^{\mathsf T}Ah+o(|h|^2)\quad(h\to0).$$
The remainder is uniform in direction. In particular $u$ is twice differentiable in the Peano sense almost everywhere.

1.1 First consider a finite convex function $f$ on an open ball. Localize on a smaller closed ball $K$ and use [F4] to obtain a finite globally Lipschitz convex $H=f$ on $K$, then set $F=H+|\cdot|^2/2$ and $g=DF^*$, which is globally one-Lipschitz and satisfies $g(q)=x$ exactly when $q\in\partial F(x)$. By [F1], the nondifferentiability set $N$ of $g$ is null; [F2] makes $g(N)$ null, and [F3] makes $g(C)$ null for the differentiable singular-derivative set $C$ of $g$. The locally Lipschitz function $F$ is differentiable outside another null set $M$ by [F1]. The union $M\cup g(N)\cup g(C)$ is null by [F6]. For $x$ in the interior of $K$ outside that union, set $p=DF(x)$. Then $g(p)=x$, $g$ is differentiable at $p$, and $B=Dg(p)$ is invertible. Full AC is used by the stated suppliers and to choose the localizations simultaneously. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, F6, F8, construct]
cases.evidence: An empty open set makes the almost-everywhere conclusion vacuous; no differentiability point must then be selected.

## Definition

**Inputs.** A nondegenerate interval $I=[a,b]$, a degree $n\ge0$, a continuous
real function $f$ on $I$, an integer exchange budget $B\in\mathbb N_0$, and an initial reference
$X=(x_0,\ldots,x_{n+1})$ with $a\le x_0<\cdots<x_{n+1}\le b$. Also supply an
exact extrema oracle for a polynomial candidate $p$. On each call it returns
one of:

- alternation$(E,y_0,\ldots,y_{n+1})$, only when $E=\|f-p\|_{\infty,I}$ and the
  returned ordered distinct nodes lie in $I$ and satisfy
  $f(y_i)-p(y_i)=\sigma(-1)^iE$ for one fixed sign $\sigma$;
- maximum$(E,y)$, only when $y\in I$, $E=\|f-p\|_{\infty,I}$ and
  $|f(y)-p(y)|=E$; or
- inconclusive, when neither exact certificate can be returned.

**Procedure.** For $k=0,\ldots,B$, solve the unique real linear system
$$p_k(x_i)+(-1)^i\lambda_k=f(x_i),\qquad 0\le i\le n+1,$$
for $p_k\in\mathcal P_n(I)$ and $\lambda_k\in\mathbb R$, using
[[lem-na-polynomial-remez-system-invertible]]. Query the oracle for $p_k$.
If it returns alternation$(0,Y)$ or maximum$(0,y)$, return exact$(p_k)$,
since either response certifies zero uniform error. If it returns
alternation$(E,Y)$ with $E>0$, return certified$(p_k,E,Y)$; the optimality
claim is discharged by [[thm-na-polynomial-equioscillation-certificate]]. If
it returns inconclusive, return oracle-inconclusive. If it returns
maximum$(E,y)$ with $E>0$ and $E=|\lambda_k|$, return certified$(p_k,E,X)$,
because the solved equations make $X$ an alternating set and the oracle
certifies the global norm. If $\lambda_k=0<E$, return zero-level-no-exchange.

In the remaining case, let $s=\operatorname{sgn}(f(y)-p_k(y))$. Find the
smallest index $i$ for which $s=\operatorname{sgn}(\lambda_k)(-1)^i$ and
replacing $x_i$ by $y$ preserves a strictly increasing reference tuple under
these tests: for $i=0$, require $a\leq y<x_1$; for $i=n+1$, require
$x_n<y\leq b$; and for $0<i<n+1$, require $x_{i-1}<y<x_{i+1}$. Thus a
global maximum at an endpoint may replace the corresponding endpoint reference
node, while distinctness and strict ordering are retained. Replace $x_i$ by
$y$ and continue. If no such index exists, return
no-order-preserving-exchange. If all $B+1$ iterations finish without a
certificate, return budget-exhausted with the last candidate and reference.

**Outputs.** The procedure returns an exact best-approximation certificate,
an exact zero-error candidate, or one of the explicit inconclusive,
zero-level, no-exchange, or budget statuses. It asserts no convergence of the
iterates. Any implementation must ensure each exact solve and oracle call
terminates.

## Statement
Assume Countable Choice. For $\tau>0$, the Fourier coefficient of $\phi_\tau$ at each integer $r$ is $\widehat\phi_\tau(r)=\sqrt{\tau}\exp(-\pi\tau r^2)$, and
$$\phi_\tau(x)=\sum_{r\in\mathbb Z}\sqrt{\tau}\exp(-\pi\tau r^2)e^{2\pi i r x}.$$
The periodized series on the left converges locally uniformly, and the Fourier series on the right converges absolutely and uniformly.

1.1 Let $h_\tau(u)=\exp(-\pi u^2/\tau)$. By [F4], induction on derivative order gives $h_\tau^{(q)}(u)=P_q(u)\exp(-\pi u^2/\tau)$ for a polynomial $P_q$. For every $m,q$, the quantity $|u|^m|P_q(u)|\exp(-\pi u^2/\tau)$ tends to zero as $|u|\to\infty$: bound the polynomial by a finite sum of powers, set $z=u^2$, and apply [F5] with $a=\pi/\tau>0$ by [F7]. On a compact interval it is bounded by continuity. Thus every seminorm in [F3] is finite and $h_\tau\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R)$. [A1, F3, F4, F5, F7, given, induction]
cases.reason: The periodizing lattice is the full integer lattice; its Gaussian terms never form an empty defining series.

## Statement
Assume Countable Choice. For $\tau>0$, the Fourier coefficient of $\phi_\tau$ at each integer $r$ is $\widehat\phi_\tau(r)=\sqrt{\tau}\exp(-\pi\tau r^2)$, and
$$\phi_\tau(x)=\sum_{r\in\mathbb Z}\sqrt{\tau}\exp(-\pi\tau r^2)e^{2\pi i r x}.$$
The periodized series on the left converges locally uniformly, and the Fourier series on the right converges absolutely and uniformly.

1.1 Let $h_\tau(u)=\exp(-\pi u^2/\tau)$. By [F4], induction on derivative order gives $h_\tau^{(q)}(u)=P_q(u)\exp(-\pi u^2/\tau)$ for a polynomial $P_q$. For every $m,q$, the quantity $|u|^m|P_q(u)|\exp(-\pi u^2/\tau)$ tends to zero as $|u|\to\infty$: bound the polynomial by a finite sum of powers, set $z=u^2$, and apply [F5] with $a=\pi/\tau>0$ by [F7]. On a compact interval it is bounded by continuity. Thus every seminorm in [F3] is finite and $h_\tau\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R)$. [A1, F3, F4, F5, F7, given, induction]
cases.evidence: Zero Fourier frequency is admitted and has coefficient the positive square root of the width.

## Statement

If a TT representation has mode sizes $n_k$ and bond sizes $r_0=r_d=1,r_1,\ldots,r_{d-1}$, its core storage is exactly
$$ \sum_{k=1}^d n_kr_{k-1}r_k $$
field entries. If $A$ and $B$ have TT cores of bond sizes $r_k$ and $s_k$, respectively, their Frobenius inner product can be computed with
$$ O\!\left(\sum_{k=1}^d n_kr_{k-1}s_{k-1}r_ks_k\right) $$
scalar arithmetic operations and $O(\max_k r_ks_k)$ additional workspace entries.

1.1 Core $G_k$ contains $r_{k-1}n_kr_k$ entries, so storing all cores requires the stated sum. The corresponding dense tensor would have $\prod_kn_k$ entries; the TT formula counts its actual core storage and by itself asserts no savings unless that sum is smaller. [F2, algebra]
cases.reason: The TT representation uses its positive mode count and terminal bonds; a zero-mode scalar convention is not asserted here.

cases.review_reason: Counting actual core entries gives exact storage, while contraction environments give the arithmetic bound.

## Statement

Use the periodic cardinal-assignment model of
[[def-ewald-pme-cardinal-assignment-model]], with integers $M_r\ge1$, order
$P\ge2$, grid size $N_g=\prod_rM_r$, a retained signed mode $k$ satisfying
$|k_r|<M_r/2$, and $D(k)\ne0$. Put $u_r=k_r/M_r$,
$a_k(t)=e^{-2\pi i k\cdot t}$, and
$$r_{k,n}=\prod_{r=1}^3 \frac{\overline{D_r(k_r+n_rM_r)}}{\overline{D_r(k_r)}},\qquad D_r(m)=e^{-\pi iPm/M_r}\operatorname{sinc}(\pi m/M_r)^P.$$
Then the single-particle assignment factor and the spread-grid coefficient obey
the absolutely convergent identities
$$b_k(t)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z^3}r_{k,n}a_{k+n\odot M}(t),\qquad z_k=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z^3}r_{k,n}\rho_{k+n\odot M},$$
where $(n\odot M)_r=n_rM_r$ and
$\rho_j=\sum_iq_i e^{-2\pi i j\cdot t_i}$. In particular
$$z_k-\rho_k=\sum_{n\ne0}r_{k,n}\rho_{k+n\odot M}.$$
The mesh coefficient also has the exact finite representation
$z_k=\sum_iq_i b_k(t_i)$, so no cell-volume or grid-size factor remains after
the displayed $\sqrt{N_g}$ conversion. The alias bound below uses only the Fourier series of
the compact spline; the lattice Poisson theorem is not applied to that spline.

For $u_r\ne0$ define
$$a_r(P,u_r)=\sum_{m\ne0}\left|\frac{u_r}{u_r+m}\right|^P, \qquad a_r(P,0)=0,\qquad A_k=\prod_{r=1}^3(1+a_r(P,u_r))-1.$$
Then $|b_k(t)-a_k(t)|\le A_k$, $|b_k(t)|\le1+A_k$, and
$|z_k-\rho_k|\le Q A_k$ for $Q=\sum_i|q_i|$. For $J\ge1$ and
$0<|u_r|<1/2$,
$$a_r(P,u_r)\le 2\frac{|u_r|^P}{(1-|u_r|)^P}\sum_{m=1}^\infty m^{-P},\qquad \sum_{|m|>J}\left|\frac{u_r}{u_r+m}\right|^P\le 2\frac{|u_r|^P}{(1-|u_r|)^P}\frac{J^{1-P}}{P-1}.$$
Thus every alias controller has a finite p-series remainder bound.
The periodic assignment also satisfies $\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal G}w_\ell(t)=1$,
so the spread-grid zero mode is $\sum_{\ell}g_\ell=\sum_iq_i=0$ for neutral data.

1.1 Define $V_1=\mathbf1_{[0,1]}$ and recursively $V_P(u)=\int_0^1V_{P-1}(u-s)ds$, so $V_P=V_{P-1}*\mathbf1_{[0,1]}$ by the convolution definition [F1]. For $P=2$, the integral is the length of $[0,1]\cap[u-1,u]$, giving $u$ on $[0,1]$, $2-u$ on $[1,2]$, and zero outside; this is the truncated-power formula. For $P\ge3$, integrate the formula for $V_{P-1}$ term by term; reindexing the second sum and applying Pascal's identity gives the stated formula for $W_P$. Thus $V_P=W_P$ for all $P\ge2$. The recursion gives nonnegativity and support in $[0,P]$. The formula gives $W_P(0)=0$, and its value at $P$ is the $P$th finite difference of the degree-$(P-1)$ polynomial $u^{P-1}$, hence is zero; therefore the zero extension is continuous at both support endpoints. Differentiating the formula on each polynomial interval and applying Pascal's identity gives $W_P'(u)=W_{P-1}(u)-W_{P-1}(u-1)$; for $P=2$ this identity holds on open intervals, with the one-sided values at integers. [F1, algebra]
cases.evidence: Grid side count one is allowed, but the retained signed mode condition then forces that coordinate frequency to zero.

## Statement

Fix one finite universe $U$ of uniquely indexed dyadic sites and weights and a dimension $d\in\{2,3\}$. For an ordered tuple of $d+2$ distinct sites whose first $d+1$ sites are affinely independent, the lexicographic lift procedure in [[def-lexicographic-lift-tie-break]] is the determinant sign of one common formal lifted configuration. Every exact nonzero power determinant retains its original sign, every exact zero has a nonzero polynomial tie determinant, and all tuples therefore receive mutually coherent signs. No numeric perturbation parameter is selected or assumed.

1.1 Expand the determinant polynomial in [F3] along its lifted-height column. It has constant coefficient equal to the original determinant and one perturbation term for each row; the coefficient of the query row's perturbation is its cofactor, which is $O_d$ up to sign. By [A1] this coefficient is nonzero, so the polynomial is not identically zero. [F1, F2, F3, A1, algebra]
cases.evidence: An exact zero determinant is precisely the tie branch, with a nonzero cofactor furnishing a first perturbation coefficient.

## Definition

Using $\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ from [[def-cartesian-gaussian-primitives-and-contractions]], for $p>0$, $P\in\mathbb R^3$, and $t,u,v\in\mathbb N_0$, the **Hermite Gaussian** is
$$\Lambda_{tuv}(x;p,P)=\frac{\partial^{t+u+v}}{\partial P_1^t\partial P_2^u\partial P_3^v}\exp(-p\|x-P\|_2^2).$$
For $\eta>0$, $P,C\in\mathbb R^3$, and $n,t,u,v\in\mathbb N_0$, define the **Boys Coulomb auxiliary function**
$$R^n_{tuv}(\eta,P-C)=(-2\eta)^n\frac{\partial^{t+u+v}}{\partial P_1^t\partial P_2^u\partial P_3^v}F_n\!\left(\eta\|P-C\|_2^2\right).$$
Each derivative is an ordinary derivative of a smooth real function of the displayed center coordinates. For the Gaussian this follows from [[thm-derivative-of-exponential]] and repeated coordinatewise product and chain rules in [[lem-derivative-algebra-and-chain-rules]]. For the Boys composition, [[thm-boys-integral-identities-series-and-incomplete-gamma]] gives $F_n^{(k)}(T)=(-1)^kF_{n+k}(T)$ by iteration on the full real extension; these derivatives are continuous by its integral representation and compact-uniform domination. The chain rules therefore also apply when $P=C$, where the Boys argument is zero. The multi-index $(t,u,v)$ records derivative order and $n$ records Boys order; both are nonnegative integers.
cases.evidence: Zero derivative orders leave the original Gaussian and Boys composition; zero center difference is explicitly admitted.

## Example

For $a,b>0$, define normalized s primitives $h_a(x)=(2a/\pi)^{3/4}e^{-a\|x\|^2}$. Their overlap is
$$S(h_a,h_b)=\left(\frac{2\sqrt{ab}}{a+b}\right)^{3/2}.$$
For $a=b$ the two-function overlap matrix has eigenvalues $2$ and $0$. For distinct exponents $a,b$ it has eigenvalues $1\pm S(h_a,h_b)$, and as $b\to a$ its condition number tends to infinity.

2.1 The Gram matrix is $\begin{pmatrix}1&S\\S&1\end{pmatrix}$, whose characteristic polynomial is $(1-\lambda)^2-S^2$, so its eigenvalues are $1\pm S$. At $a=b$, $S=1$ and the lower eigenvalue is zero. For $a\ne b$, $2\sqrt{ab}<a+b$, hence $0<S<1$; continuity of the displayed formula gives $S\to1$ as $b\to a$, and therefore $(1+S)/(1-S)\to\infty$. [given, algebra] ∎
cases.evidence: Equal positive exponents produce an overlap eigenvalue zero, and the example explicitly permits that singular Gram matrix.

## Definition

On a neighborhood where an eigenvector field $r_i$ is $C^2$, the local
$i$-rarefaction curve through $u_0$ is the unique local solution
$$\frac{dR_i}{d\sigma}(\sigma;u_0)=r_i(R_i(\sigma;u_0)),\qquad R_i(0;u_0)=u_0.$$
The parameter $\sigma$ is the signed integral-curve parameter for the chosen
normalization of $r_i$. Existence on a common small interval for nearby $u_0$
follows from [[cor-uniform-picard-lindelof-for-nearby-initial-values]]; the
$C^2$ flow on a compact local tube follows from
[[thm-c2-ode-flow-on-common-tube]]. No global integral curve is asserted.

## Statement

When $S_L<0<S_R$, the HLL intermediate state
$$u_* =\frac{S_Ru_R-S_Lu_L-(f_R-f_L)}{S_R-S_L}$$
satisfies the Rankine–Hugoniot balance across both waves, and its flux at
$\xi=0$ is the middle formula in [[def-hll-two-wave-flux]]. For equal states
the HLL flux is consistent. A finite-volume update using the same HLL flux at
each periodic interface is conservative: for any finite periodic array with
adjacent pairs in the flux domain, define
$$U_j^{new}=U_j-\nu\bigl(\widehat f_{\rm HLL}(U_j,U_{j+1})-\widehat f_{\rm HLL}(U_{j-1},U_j)\bigr).$$
Here $n\ge1$. The result holds for any scalar $\nu$ and assumes the supplied speeds; it does
not prove that they enclose a nonlinear Riemann fan.

1.1 Put $D=S_R-S_L>0$. Direct subtraction gives $u_*-u_L=(S_R(u_R-u_L)-(f_R-f_L))/D$ and $u_R-u_*=(-S_L(u_R-u_L)+(f_R-f_L))/D$. Define $f_*=f_L+S_L(u_*-u_L)$; substitution gives $f_*=(S_Rf_L-S_Lf_R+S_LS_R(u_R-u_L))/D$. Then $f_*-f_L=S_L(u_*-u_L)$ and $f_R-f_*=S_R(u_R-u_*)$, which are [F2] for both jumps. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

## Definition

Fix constant transport velocity $\beta\in\mathbb R^d$ and SBP data from [[def-pe04-diagonal-norm-sbp-element-data]]. For each cell $K$, let $U_K(t)$ be the vector of nodal values, $Q_{K,\ell}=H_KD_{K,\ell}$, and $U_{K,F}=R_{K,F}U_K$. Set $b_{K,F}=\beta\cdot n_{K,F}$. At each interior face, use the trace from the cell with positive outward speed when $b_{K,F}>0$, and the neighboring trace when $b_{K,F}<0$; at boundary faces use the inflow data on $b_{K,F}<0$ and the interior trace on $b_{K,F}\ge0$. Denote this upwind scalar trace by $\widehat U_{K,F}$.

The **upwind SBP-SAT semidiscretization** is
$$H_K\dot U_K+\sum_{\ell=1}^d\beta_\ell Q_{K,\ell}U_K+\sum_{F\subset\partial K}R_{K,F}^{T}M_{K,F}\,b_{K,F}(\widehat U_{K,F}-U_{K,F})=0.$$
The sign of the SAT correction is fixed by this equation. The definition is spatial only and makes no fully discrete claim.
cases.reason: SBP data supply a finite nodal vector on each actual mesh cell; an empty spatial discretization is not defined.

At each interior face, use the trace from the cell with positive outward speed when $b_{K,F}>0$, and the neighboring trace when $b_{K,F}<0$; at boundary faces use the inflow data on $b_{K,F}<0$ and the interior trace on $b_{K,F}\ge0$. $$H_K\dot U_K+\sum_{\ell=1}^d\beta_\ell Q_{K,\ell}U_K+\sum_{F\subset\partial K}R_{K,F}^{T}M_{K,F}\,b_{K,F}(\widehat U_{K,F}-U_{K,F})=0.$$
The sign of the SAT correction is fixed by this equation. The definition is spatial only and makes no fully discrete claim.

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded open
set. Suppose $u_n\in H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$,
$u_n\to u$ strongly in $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$, and
$\sup_n\|\operatorname{curl}u_n\|_2<\infty$. Then a subsequence of the
curls converges weakly in $L^2$ to $\operatorname{curl}u$, the limit $u$
belongs to $H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$, and in fact
$u\in H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$.

1.1 The graph of distributional curl is closed in $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)\times L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$: if $v_j\to v$ and $\operatorname{curl}v_j\to w$ in $L^2$, [F3] gives $\int_\Omega w\cdot\varphi\,dx=\int_\Omega v\cdot\operatorname{curl}\varphi\,dx$ for each test $\varphi$, so $\operatorname{curl}v=w$. By [F1] the product is Hilbert, hence its closed graph is Hilbert with the graph inner product. Thus $H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$ is a Hilbert space. [F1, F3, given, algebra]
cases.evidence: If the bounded open set is empty, its L2 graph is the zero space and the sequence conclusion is immediate.

## Definition

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega$ and $\mathcal T$ be as in
[[def-crouzeix-raviart-global-space]], let $V:=H^1_0(\Omega)$, let
$V_h:=V_h^{CR,0}$, and let $f\in L^2(\Omega)$. The exact Poisson form and
load are
$$a(u,v):=\int_\Omega\nabla u\cdot\nabla v\,dx,\qquad F(v):=\int_\Omega f v\,dx\quad (u,v\in V).$$
An exact solution is a $u\in V$ satisfying $a(u,v)=F(v)$ for every $v\in V$.
For $v_h,w_h\in V_h$, define the broken form and discrete load by
$$a_h(v_h,w_h):=\sum_{K\in\mathcal T}\int_K\nabla v_h\cdot\nabla w_h\,dx, \qquad F_h(w_h):=\int_\Omega f w_h\,dx.$$
The discrete problem is to find $u_h\in V_h$ such that
$a_h(u_h,w_h)=F_h(w_h)$ for every $w_h\in V_h$.

Put $X_h:=V+V_h$. For each cell facet $F\subset\partial K$, let
$\gamma_{F,K}$ denote the trace supplied by
[[lem-crouzeix-raviart-simplex-traces-and-green-identity]].
For $z\in X_h$ and $w_h\in V_h$, define the comparison-space extension
$$\widetilde a_h(z,w_h):=\sum_{K\in\mathcal T}\int_K \nabla(z|_K)\cdot\nabla w_h\,dx.$$
Each restriction $z|_K$ belongs to $H^1(K)$, and this extension agrees with
$a_h$ when $z\in V_h$.

On an interior facet
$F=K^+\cap K^-$ choose either ordering and define
$[z]_F:=\gamma_{F,K^+}z-\gamma_{F,K^-}z$; on a boundary facet of $K$ set
$[z]_F:=\gamma_{F,K}z$. The mesh-dependent comparison expression is
$$\|z\|_{\sharp,h}^2:= \sum_{K\in\mathcal T}\|\nabla(z|_K)\|_{L^2(K)}^2+ \sum_{F\in\mathcal F^\circ\cup\mathcal F^\partial} h_F^{-1}\|[z]_F\|_{L^2(F)}^2,\qquad z\in X_h.$$
The next items prove the required definiteness, stability, and consistency
properties; this definition makes no assertion that $V_h\subset V$.

## Statement

For every interior facet $F$, define $\phi_F$ to equal $\phi_{K,F}$ on each
cell $K$ incident to $F$ and zero on all other cells, where
$\phi_{K,F}$ is the local shape polynomial of
[[def-crouzeix-raviart-local-p1-element]]. Then
$\{\phi_F:F\in\mathcal F^\circ\}$ is a basis of the space in
[[def-crouzeix-raviart-global-space]]. The face mean $\bar v_F:=|F|^{-1}\int_F
v_K\,dS$ is single-valued for $v\in V_h^{CR,0}$ and
$\dim V_h^{CR,0}=|\mathcal F^\circ|$.

1.1 The two traces of $v\in V_h^{CR,0}$ on an interior facet have equal integrals by definition, so $\bar v_F$ is single-valued. For an interior facet $F$, the function $\phi_F$ has mean one on $F$, mean zero on every other facet of each incident cell by [F1], and is zero on cells not incident to $F$. Thus $\phi_F\in V_h^{CR,0}$ and $\bar\phi_{F,G}=\delta_{FG}$ for all interior facets $G$. [F1, given, algebra]

## Example

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. For a fixed direction $d\in S^2$, consider the incident plane wave $g_k(\omega)=e^{ikd\cdot\omega}$ on the unit sphere. Let $\Pi_L$ denote projection onto degrees $0,\ldots,L$. For each fixed $L$, its value at the forward direction tends to zero as $k\to\infty$, whereas $g_k(d)=e^{ik}$ has modulus one. Thus a fixed angular cutoff has forward error tending to one; uniform high-frequency accuracy below one requires the cutoff to tend to infinity.

1.1 By [F1] and [F2], $(\Pi_Lg_k)(d)=\sum_{\ell=0}^{L}\frac{2\ell+1}{2}\int_{-1}^1e^{ikt}P_\ell(t)dt$. For a fixed polynomial $P_\ell$, integration by parts gives $\left|\int_{-1}^{1}e^{ikt}P_\ell(t)dt\right|\le\frac{|P_\ell(1)|+|P_\ell(-1)|+\int_{-1}^1|P_\ell'(t)|dt}{k}$. Summing finitely many terms yields $|(\Pi_Lg_k)(d)|\le C_L/k$ for a finite constant $C_L$ independent of $k$. [F1, F2, given, algebra]
cases.reason: A direction on the unit sphere and a nonnegative cutoff are supplied; the sphere is not empty.

## Statement

Let $\rho^+_j=h^{-d}\sum_pq_pw_j(X_p)$ be the deposited density before background subtraction for an admissible algebraic shape $w_j$ of [[def-periodic-pic-shape-assignment-and-gather]], and let $G_X$ be its scalar potential gather. For every grid scalar $\phi$,
$$ \langle\rho^+,\phi\rangle_h=\sum_{p=1}^P q_p(G_X\phi)_p . $$ For the neutralized density $\rho=\rho^+-Q/L^d$ the corresponding identity is $$ \langle\rho,\phi\rangle_h=\sum_pq_p(G_X\phi)_p-Q\bar\phi . $$
Thus the background term vanishes in the zero-mean potential gauge.

1.1 Substitute [F2] into the left pairing and cancel $h^d h^{-d}$: $\langle\rho^+,\phi\rangle_h =h^d\sum_jh^{-d}\sum_pq_pw_j(X_p)\phi_j =\sum_pq_p\sum_jw_j(X_p)\phi_j .$ The finite inner sum is $(G_X\phi)_p$ by [F2], proving the first identity. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

Let $R=\prod_{i=1}^m[a_i,b_i]$ be reaction-inward for $F$ from [[def-reaction-vector-field-and-quasipositivity]]. Assume for each $i$ there is a coordinate Lipschitz constant $L_i\ge0$ such that $|F_i(z)-F_i(w)|\le L_i|z_i-w_i|$ whenever $z,w\in R$ differ only in coordinate $i$. Define
$$
\tau_R=\min_{i:L_i>0}L_i^{-1},
$$
with $\tau_R=+\infty$ if every $L_i=0$. For $z\in R$ and $0\le\tau\le\tau_R$, the forward-Euler reaction step $z^+=z+\tau F(z)$ lies in $R$. For every conservation vector $c$ on $R$, $c^Tz^+=c^Tz$; for every dissipation vector, $c^Tz^+\le c^Tz$.

1.1 Fix coordinate $i$ and keep the other coordinates of $z$ fixed. Let $z^-$ replace $z_i$ by $a_i$. By [F1], $F_i(z^-)\ge0$; hence [A1] gives $F_i(z)\ge-L_i(z_i-a_i)$. Similarly, let $z^+$ replace $z_i$ by $b_i$. Then [F1] and [A1] give $F_i(z)\le L_i(b_i-z_i)$. [A1, F1, given, construct]
cases.reason: The reaction rectangle has ordered coordinate intervals and supplied state, so a nonempty state is already given.

cases.input_text: The statement excludes the degenerate interval, domain, or matrix case, so no additional degenerate branch is claimed.
cases.review_reason: Zero coordinate Lipschitz constants force the corresponding reaction component to vanish; the empty positive-index minimum is explicitly infinity.

## Statement

Let $R=\prod_{i=1}^m[a_i,b_i]$ be the reaction-inward rectangle of [[def-reaction-invariant-rectangle]]. Assume $F$ from [[def-reaction-vector-field-and-quasipositivity]] is continuously differentiable on an open neighborhood of $R$, and its derivative is bounded on some closed neighborhood of $R$. For any $z_0\in R$, the IVP $z'=F(z)$ has a unique solution for every $t\ge0$, and $z(t)\in R$. If $c$ is a conservation vector on $R$, then $c^Tz(t)=c^Tz_0$; if it is a dissipation vector, then $c^Tz(t)$ is nonincreasing. The lower-face condition is quasi-positivity when $a_i=0$; upper-face inwardness remains a separate hypothesis.

1.1 Let $z(t)$ be the unique local solution from [F3] and let $p(t)$ be the coordinatewise projection of $z(t)$ onto $R$. While $z(t)\in R_\delta$, define $V(t)=\sum_i((a_i-z_i(t))_+^2+(z_i(t)-b_i)_+^2)$, where $x_+=\max(x,0)$. The squared positive-part function is continuously differentiable. If $z_i<a_i$, then $p_i=a_i$ and [F1], [A1] give $F_i(z)\ge F_i(p)-L\|z-p\|\ge-L\|z-p\|$; if $z_i>b_i$, then $p_i=b_i$ and $F_i(z)\le F_i(p)+L\|z-p\|\le L\|z-p\|$. Differentiating the active terms of $V$ therefore yields $V'(t)\le C_m L V(t)$ for a finite constant $C_m$ depending only on $m$. [A1, F1, F3, given, algebra]
cases.reason: A supplied initial state in the rectangle establishes nonemptiness before the local IVP is invoked.

cases.input_text: The statement excludes the degenerate interval, domain, or matrix case, so no additional degenerate branch is claimed.
cases.review_reason: Degenerate coordinate widths remain invariant because both face signs force zero motion in that coordinate.

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Fix $0<r_0<1$. Use a linear radial coordinate $\rho(s)=r_0+(1-r_0)s$ and a rational quadratic angular curve with control points $Q_0=(1,0)$, $Q_1=(1,1)$, $Q_2=(0,1)$ and weights $(1,1/\sqrt2,1)$. Tensor their bases, use control points $P_{ij}=r_iQ_j$ for $r_i\in\{r_0,1\}$, and tensor weights $w_{ij}=w_j$. The resulting patch maps $[0,1]^2$ bijectively onto $\{(x,y):r_0\le\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\le1,\ x,y\ge0\}$ with strictly positive Jacobian, and its exact map satisfies the norm-equivalence hypotheses of [[lem-isogeometric-pullback-energy-norm-equivalence]].

1.1 Put $a=\sqrt2$ and $x_0(t)=(1-t)^2+a t(1-t),\qquad y_0(t)=t^2+a t(1-t),\qquad D(t)=(1-t)^2+a t(1-t)+t^2.$ The weighted middle Bernstein coefficient is $2(1/\sqrt2)t(1-t)=a t(1-t)$, so the angular map is $(X,Y)=(x_0/D,y_0/D)$. Direct expansion gives $x_0^2+y_0^2-D^2=-2t^2(1-t)^2+a^2t^2(1-t)^2=0,$ so $X^2+Y^2=1$; also $X,Y\ge0$ and $D>0$. The tensor-product weights and controls therefore give $F(s,t)=(\rho(s)X(t),\rho(s)Y(t))$. [F1, F2, given, algebra]
cases.reason: The image is a nonempty quarter annulus because its inner radius lies strictly between zero and one.

cases.input_text: No zero-valued input is a boundary case of this claim.
cases.review_reason: The origin and zero inner radius are excluded; the determinant is uniformly positive on the whole parameter square.

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Fix $0<r_0<1$. Use a linear radial coordinate $\rho(s)=r_0+(1-r_0)s$ and a rational quadratic angular curve with control points $Q_0=(1,0)$, $Q_1=(1,1)$, $Q_2=(0,1)$ and weights $(1,1/\sqrt2,1)$. Tensor their bases, use control points $P_{ij}=r_iQ_j$ for $r_i\in\{r_0,1\}$, and tensor weights $w_{ij}=w_j$. The resulting patch maps $[0,1]^2$ bijectively onto $\{(x,y):r_0\le\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\le1,\ x,y\ge0\}$ with strictly positive Jacobian, and its exact map satisfies the norm-equivalence hypotheses of [[lem-isogeometric-pullback-energy-norm-equivalence]].

3.1 The Jacobian is $\det DF(s,t)=\rho'(s)\rho(s)(XY'-YX')=(1-r_0)\rho(s)\frac{\sqrt2}{D(t)}>0.$ On the closed square, $\rho\ge r_0>0$ and $D$ is continuous and positive, so this determinant has positive minimum and finite maximum; $DF$ is continuous and bounded, and the inverse matrix is bounded by its cofactor formula divided by the positive determinant. The physical inverse first recovers $\rho=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ and the angle $\theta=\operatorname{atan2}(y,x)$. This angle is Lipschitz on the annular sector because $\rho\ge r_0$, and the inverse parameter $t(\theta)$ is Lipschitz because $\theta'(t)=\sqrt2/D(t)$ has a positive minimum. Together with the linear inverse for $s$, this makes $F^{-1}$ Lipschitz; bounded $DF$ makes $F$ Lipschitz. The quarter annulus has a finite piecewise smooth Lipschitz boundary, so all admissibility hypotheses in [F1] hold. Applying [F3] gives the announced pullback norm equivalence. [A1, F1, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, given, algebra] ∎
cases.reason: Positive radial width and positive rational denominator prevent singular geometry.

cases.review_reason: All four parameter edges are included, with angular endpoints traversing the first-quadrant circle arc exactly once.

$$|U_g(x)|\le C_{d,s}\|g\|_{L^2_s}\qquad(x\in\mathbb R^d).$$

## Statement

Let $p\ge0$ be an integer, let $Y=(y_1,\ldots,y_N)$ be distinct and $(p+1)$-unisolvent for $\Pi_p(\mathbb R^d)$, and let $K$ be a real strictly conditionally positive-definite kernel of order $p+1$. Fix a center $x$, an ordered basis $p_1,\ldots,p_J$ of $\Pi_p$, and a homogeneous constant-coefficient differential functional $L$ of order $t\le p$ for which all section derivatives in [[alg-augmented-rbf-finite-difference-weights]] exist. Let $(w,v)$ be the exact output of that procedure and put $r_Y=\max_i|y_i-x|$. Then the procedure returns success, and for every $q\in\Pi_p$,
$$\sum_{i=1}^Nw_iq(y_i)=Lq(x).$$
If $f\in C^{p+1}(U)$ on an open convex set $U$ containing the compact convex hull $H=\operatorname{conv}\{x,y_1,\ldots,y_N\}$, then
$$\left|\sum_iw_if(y_i)-Lf(x)\right|\le C_{d,p}\left(\sum_i|w_i|\right)r_Y^{p+1}\max_{|\alpha|=p+1}\sup_{z\in H}|D^\alpha f(z)|.$$
Consequently, a separately proved bound $\sum_i|w_i|\le C_wr_Y^{-t}$ yields the order $C_{d,p}C_wr_Y^{p+1-t}$ truncation bound. Unisolvence alone is not asserted to provide this weight-norm bound.

1.1 Let $M$ be the augmented matrix and $g$ its right side in [F1]. It is square and invertible by [F2]. Initially the leading $0\times0$ pivot block is invertible. Inductively suppose the first $k-1$ pivots have been nonzero. After their row swaps and elimination, the row-equivalent matrix has block form $\begin{bmatrix}U&B\\0&S\end{bmatrix}$ with $U$ invertible and $S$ the remaining Schur complement. The block matrix is invertible, so $S$ is invertible: if $Sz=0$, then $(-U^{-1}Bz,z)$ would be a nonzero vector in its kernel. If the first column of $S$ were zero, its first coordinate vector would be a nonzero kernel vector. Thus the finite set of remaining entries in column $k$ contains a nonzero entry, and the algorithm's least-index rule finds a nonzero pivot. Row swaps and adding multiples of pivot rows are invertible elementary row operations, so they preserve the solution set. After $N+J$ pivots the matrix is upper triangular with nonzero diagonal, and descending substitution returns the unique solution. Therefore the singular-system status is unreachable under the hypotheses. [F1, F2, induction, algebra]

## Statement

Let $p\ge0$ be an integer, let $Y=(y_1,\ldots,y_N)$ be distinct and $(p+1)$-unisolvent for $\Pi_p(\mathbb R^d)$, and let $K$ be a real strictly conditionally positive-definite kernel of order $p+1$. Fix a center $x$, an ordered basis $p_1,\ldots,p_J$ of $\Pi_p$, and a homogeneous constant-coefficient differential functional $L$ of order $t\le p$ for which all section derivatives in [[alg-augmented-rbf-finite-difference-weights]] exist. Let $(w,v)$ be the exact output of that procedure and put $r_Y=\max_i|y_i-x|$. Then the procedure returns success, and for every $q\in\Pi_p$,
$$\sum_{i=1}^Nw_iq(y_i)=Lq(x).$$
If $f\in C^{p+1}(U)$ on an open convex set $U$ containing the compact convex hull $H=\operatorname{conv}\{x,y_1,\ldots,y_N\}$, then
$$\left|\sum_iw_if(y_i)-Lf(x)\right|\le C_{d,p}\left(\sum_i|w_i|\right)r_Y^{p+1}\max_{|\alpha|=p+1}\sup_{z\in H}|D^\alpha f(z)|.$$
Consequently, a separately proved bound $\sum_i|w_i|\le C_wr_Y^{-t}$ yields the order $C_{d,p}C_wr_Y^{p+1-t}$ truncation bound. Unisolvence alone is not asserted to provide this weight-norm bound.

1.1 Let $M$ be the augmented matrix and $g$ its right side in [F1]. It is square and invertible by [F2]. Initially the leading $0\times0$ pivot block is invertible. Inductively suppose the first $k-1$ pivots have been nonzero. After their row swaps and elimination, the row-equivalent matrix has block form $\begin{bmatrix}U&B\\0&S\end{bmatrix}$ with $U$ invertible and $S$ the remaining Schur complement. The block matrix is invertible, so $S$ is invertible: if $Sz=0$, then $(-U^{-1}Bz,z)$ would be a nonzero vector in its kernel. If the first column of $S$ were zero, its first coordinate vector would be a nonzero kernel vector. Thus the finite set of remaining entries in column $k$ contains a nonzero entry, and the algorithm's least-index rule finds a nonzero pivot. Row swaps and adding multiples of pivot rows are invertible elementary row operations, so they preserve the solution set. After $N+J$ pivots the matrix is upper triangular with nonzero diagonal, and descending substitution returns the unique solution. Therefore the singular-system status is unreachable under the hypotheses. [F1, F2, induction, algebra]

## Statement

For Hermitian $G,H\succeq0$, define $\Phi_G(X)=X(I+GX)^{-1}$ and $f(X)=H+A^*\Phi_G(X)A$ on $X\succeq0$. One doubling step in [[alg-finite-budget-structure-preserving-doubling-for-dare]] is well-defined, preserves $G_j,H_j\succeq0$, and its updated triple satisfies
$$f\circ f(X)=H_1+A_1^*X(I+G_1X)^{-1}A_1,$$
where
$$A_1=A(I+GH)^{-1}A,\quad G_1=G+A(I+GH)^{-1}GA^*,\quad H_1=H+A^*H(I+GH)^{-1}A.$$
Consequently, if $f_0=f$ and the recurrence is iterated, then $H_j=f^{2^j}(0)$.

1.1 If $(I+GH)v=0$, then multiplication by $v^*H$ gives $v^*Hv+(Hv)^*G(Hv)=0.$ Both terms are nonnegative, so $Hv=0$ and then $v=0$. Thus $I+GH$ is invertible; the same argument applies to $I+HG$. The identities $(I+GH)^{-1}G=G(I+HG)^{-1} =G^{1/2}(I+G^{1/2}HG^{1/2})^{-1}G^{1/2},$ $H(I+GH)^{-1}=(I+HG)^{-1}H =H^{1/2}(I+H^{1/2}GH^{1/2})^{-1}H^{1/2}$ follow by multiplication and the push-through identity. Their middle matrices are positive definite, so both displayed products are Hermitian positive semidefinite. Therefore the updates in [F1] give $G_1,H_1\succeq0$ and use only an inverse already proved to exist. [F1, F3, algebra]

## Statement

Fix real $x>0$ and integer $N\ge0$. Set
$I_N=[0,(N+1)/(2x)]$, and for $k=N-1,\ldots,0$ define

$$I_k=\left[\frac{k+1}{2(x+\sup I_{k+1})}, \frac{k+1}{2(x+\inf I_{k+1})}\right].$$

from [[lem-erfcx-moment-recurrence]]. Therefore

$$\operatorname{erfcx}(x)\in \left[\frac1{\sqrt\pi(x+\sup I_0)}, \frac1{\sqrt\pi(x+\inf I_0)}\right].$$

## Statement

For $f(x)=e^{-x^2}$ on $\mathbb R$, use the sinh–sinh mode of [[alg-double-exponential-trapezoid]]. Its transformed function is
$$\Phi(t)=\frac\pi2\cosh t\,\cosh u(t)\,e^{-\sinh^2u(t)},\qquad u(t)=\frac\pi2\sinh t.$$
Then $\int_{\mathbb R}\Phi(t)dt=\sqrt\pi$. There is $T>0$ such that $|\Phi(t)|\le e^{-e^{|t|}}$ for $|t|\ge T$, so if $N_\pm h\ge T$, the omitted finite-sum tail is at most
$$e^{-e^{N_-h}}+e^{-e^{N_+h}}.$$
However, the complex extension of this transformed Gaussian does not satisfy the uniform exponential-decay hypothesis of [[thm-analytic-strip-trapezoid-error]] on any nonzero horizontal substrip. Thus this example certifies its truncation tail but does not claim a full discretization-plus-tail error bound.

1.1 On the real axis, $x'(t)=(\pi/2)\cosh t\cosh u(t)>0$. As $t\to\pm\infty$, $x(t)\to\pm\infty$. We show the tail envelope for $t\to+\infty$; evenness gives the left tail. For $t\ge1$, $\sinh t\ge c e^t$ with $c=(1-e^{-2})/2>0$, so $u(t)\ge c_1e^t$ for $c_1=\pi c/2$. For $u\ge1$, $\sinh u\ge c e^u$, hence $x(t)^2\ge c^2e^{2u(t)}\ge c^2e^{2c_1e^t}$. Also $u(t)\le(\pi/4)e^t$ and $\cosh t\le e^t$, $\cosh u\le e^u$, so for a fixed constant $C'>0$ and all sufficiently large $t$, $(\pi/2)\cosh t\cosh u(t)\le e^{C'e^t}$. Put $v=e^t$. By [F8], $v\to\infty$, and [F9] implies $c^2e^{2c_1v}/v\to\infty$. Thus $x(t)^2$ eventually exceeds both $2C'e^t$ and $2e^t$. It follows that $\Phi(t)\le e^{C'e^t-x(t)^2}\le e^{-x(t)^2/2}\le e^{-e^t}$ for all sufficiently large $t$. [F1, F8, F9, algebra]

positive densities $\rho_L,\rho_R$. Set
$E_K=p_0/(\gamma-1)+\rho_Ku_0^2/2$ and

Fix $\gamma>1$, pressure $p_0>0$, velocity $u_0\in\mathbb R$, and distinct
positive densities $\rho_L,\rho_R$. Set
$E_K=p_0/(\gamma-1)+\rho_Ku_0^2/2$ and
$U_K=(\rho_K,\rho_Ku_0,E_K)$ for $K=L,R$.

1.1 Both states are admissible because $\rho_K>0$ and their internal energy is $p_0/(\gamma-1)>0$. For either state, $F(U_K)-u_0U_K=(0,p_0,u_0p_0)$; subtracting the two identities gives $F(U_R)-F(U_L)=u_0(U_R-U_L)$, the Rankine–Hugoniot equality at speed $u_0$. [given, F1, algebra]
cases.reason: A general Rankine–Hugoniot jump need not be a linearly degenerate contact with common pressure and velocity.

## Statement

Let $r_i$ be a $C^1$ genuinely nonlinear field on a neighborhood, with
$D\lambda_i(u)r_i(u)$ of constant nonzero sign. If $\sigma\ne0$ satisfies
$\sigma D\lambda_i(u_0)r_i(u_0)>0$ and is sufficiently small, then the
left/right data $u_0,R_i(\sigma;u_0)$ are connected by a centered rarefaction
fan. It is a self-similar weak solution with those Riemann data.

1.1 Along the curve, $\frac{d}{ds}\lambda_i(R_i(s;u_0))=D\lambda_i(R_i(s;u_0))r_i(R_i(s;u_0))$ keeps its nonzero sign. Therefore the map $s\mapsto\lambda_i(R_i(s;u_0))$ is strictly monotone, and for each speed between its endpoint values there is a unique curve parameter $s$. Since $\sigma D\lambda_i(u_0)r_i(u_0)>0$ and the sign remains constant, $\lambda_i(R_i(\sigma;u_0))>\lambda_i(u_0)$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]
cases.reason: The fan joins two supplied nearby states along a curve through the initial state.

## Statement

Fix $\gamma>1$ and $\varepsilon>0$. The ideal-gas admissible set
$$\mathcal G_\gamma=\left\{(\rho,m,E):\rho>0,\ E-\frac{m^2}{2\rho}>0\right\}$$
and the positive-margin set $K_{\gamma,\varepsilon}$ from
[[def-pe03-euler-positive-margin-domain]] are convex, and
$K_{\gamma,\varepsilon}$ is closed in $\mathbb R^3$.

1.1 Let $U_k=(\rho_k,m_k,E_k)\in\mathcal G_\gamma$ for $k=1,2$ and $0\le\theta\le1$. Put $\rho_\theta=\theta\rho_1+(1-\theta)\rho_2$ and similarly define $m_\theta,E_\theta$. Weighted Cauchy–Schwarz applied to $m_\theta=\sqrt{\theta\rho_1}(\sqrt\theta m_1/\sqrt{\rho_1})+\sqrt{(1-\theta)\rho_2}(\sqrt{1-\theta}m_2/\sqrt{\rho_2})$ gives $m_\theta^2\le\rho_\theta\bigl(\theta m_1^2/\rho_1+(1-\theta)m_2^2/\rho_2\bigr)$. Thus $\rho_\theta>0$ and $E_\theta-m_\theta^2/(2\rho_\theta)\ge\theta(E_1-m_1^2/(2\rho_1))+(1-\theta)(E_2-m_2^2/(2\rho_2))>0$. Therefore $\mathcal G_\gamma$ is convex. [given, F1, algebra]
cases.evidence: The margin set is nonempty, for example zero momentum and sufficiently large positive density and energy.

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice and let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be open. Every real vector field $w\in H^1_0(D;\mathbb R^d)$ belongs to $H_0(\operatorname{div};D)$, where the latter is the kernel of the weak normal trace. In particular, $\operatorname{div}w\in L^2(D)$ and its weak normal trace vanishes on the whole boundary trace quotient.

1.1 Since each component of $w$ and each first weak derivative is in $L^2(D)$ by [F1], the finite sum $\operatorname{div}w=\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_jw_j$ lies in $L^2(D)$. Thus $w\in H(\operatorname{div};D)$ by its definition. [F1, construct, algebra]
cases.evidence: An empty open domain has only zero Sobolev classes and the inclusion is immediate.

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. For $d\in\{2,3\}$ and $V=H^1_0(D;\mathbb R^d)$ on a bounded Lipschitz domain, the form in [[def-na-evolutionary-skew-convective-form]] is a continuous real trilinear map $V^3\to\mathbb R$, is skew in its last two slots, and satisfies
$$|c(a;b,w)|\le C_D\|a\|_{L^2}^{1/2}\|\nabla a\|_{L^2}^{1/2}\|\nabla b\|_{L^2}\|\nabla w\|_{L^2}.$$
Consequently, if $u\in L^\infty(0,T;L^2)\cap L^2(0,T;V)$, then $c(u;u,\cdot)\in L^{4/3}(0,T;V^*)$. If $\operatorname{div}u=0$ and $d=2$, the sharper estimate
$$|c(u;u,w)|\le C_D\|u\|_{L^2}\|\nabla u\|_{L^2}\|\nabla w\|_{L^2}$$
holds. If $\operatorname{div}a=0$, the skew form agrees with the advective form $\int_D(a\cdot\nabla)b\cdot w$.

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice and the SIPDG setting of [[def-sipdg-bilinear-form-and-energy-norm]]. Let $u$ satisfy all hypotheses of [[thm-sipdg-exact-consistency]], and let $u_h\in V_h^{\rm br}$ satisfy $a_h(u_h,v_h)=\ell_h(v_h)$ for all $v_h\in V_h^{\rm br}$. Set $e:=u-u_h$, let $V:=H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb R)=W_0^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ as in [[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]], and let $h:=\max_{K\in\mathcal T}h_K$, with $0<h\le\ell_\Omega:=\operatorname{diam}(\Omega)$. Suppose $s\in(1/2,1]$ and a dual solution $z_e\in V$ exists satisfying
$$\sum_{K\in\mathcal T}\int_KA_K\nabla v\cdot\nabla z_e\,dx=\int_\Omega ve\,dx\qquad(v\in V),$$
with the following properties:

1. Its one-sided normal coefficient-flux traces are in $L^2(F)$ in the weak Green sense defining $\mathcal D_h$. In the branch $s=1$, assume also $z_e|_K\in H^2(K)$ on every cell, with matching interior value traces, zero boundary value trace, and matching interior normal coefficient fluxes; then [[lem-sipdg-adjoint-consistency-h2]] gives $a_h(e,z_e)=\|e\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2$. In the branch $s<1$, assume this adjoint-consistency identity as an additional hypothesis. The weak dual equation gives $\operatorname{div}(A_K\nabla z_e)|_K=-e|_K\in L^2(K)$, so the stated flux and trace conditions place $z_e$ in the form domain $\mathcal D_h$ of [[def-sipdg-bilinear-form-and-energy-norm]].
2. The specified normed dual-regularity space $\mathcal R_s$ is a subspace of $V\cap\mathcal D_h$, and $\|z_e\|_{\mathcal R_s}\le C_{\rm reg}\|e\|_{L^2(\Omega)}$ for some $C_{\rm reg}\ge0$.
3. There is $z_h\in V_h^{\rm br}$ such that
$$\|z_e-z_h\|_{DG,*}\le C_{\rm app}h^s\ell_\Omega^{1-s}\|z_e\|_{\mathcal R_s}.$$
Here $C_{\rm app}\ge0$.

Then
$$\|e\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\le (2+2\gamma^{-1/2})C_{\rm app}C_{\rm reg}h^s\ell_\Omega^{1-s}\|e\|_{DG,*}.$$
The theorem retains the dual regularity exponent and the half-order face-flux contribution in $\|\cdot\|_{DG,*}$. It does not infer the dual approximation estimate or adjoint-consistency identity from elliptic regularity alone.

1.1 The result is immediate if $\|e\|_{L^2}=0$. Otherwise choose $z_h$ from the stated approximation hypothesis. For $s=1$, [F3] gives $a_h(e,z_e)=\|e\|_{L^2}^2$ under the stated piecewise-$H^2$ and trace-matching hypotheses; for $s<1$ this identity is [A1]. Exact consistency plus the discrete equation give $a_h(e,z_h)=0$ by [F1]. Hence $\|e\|_{L^2}^2=a_h(e,z_e-z_h)$. [F1, F3, F4, A1, given, choose]
cases.reason: Galerkin orthogonality and the assumed adjoint identity imply the displayed L2 estimate.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. On the $C^2$ surface of [[def-bem-smooth-helmholtz-combined-field-operator]], the extensions of [[lem-bem-smooth-trace-and-helmholtz-layer-extension]] satisfy, for $\phi\in H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$ and $\lambda\in H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)$,
$$\gamma^-D_k\phi-\gamma^+D_k\phi=-\phi,\qquad \partial_n^-D_k\phi-\partial_n^+D_k\phi=0,$$
$$\gamma^-S_k\lambda-\gamma^+S_k\lambda=0,\qquad \partial_n^-S_k\lambda-\partial_n^+S_k\lambda=\lambda.$$
Trace and conormal equalities hold in $H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$ and $H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)$, respectively; both conormals use the same normal $n$ pointing out of $\Omega^-$.

1.1 For any piecewise $H^1$ Helmholtz solution $u$ with jumps $[\gamma u]=\gamma^-u-\gamma^+u$ and $[q]=q^- -q^+$, apply the two weak Green identities of [F1] to a compactly supported smooth test $v$. The outer artificial boundary contributes zero, and the opposite orientations of the inner boundary give $\langle P_ku,v\rangle=\langle[q],v|_\Gamma\rangle_{\rm bil}-\int_\Gamma[\gamma u]\partial_nv\,dS$. The subscript indicates the complex-bilinear version of weak duality; conjugating the test converts this to the sesquilinear convention. For $u=D_k\phi$, the differentiated kernel source identity is $\langle P_kD_k\phi,v\rangle=\int_\Gamma\phi\partial_nv\,dS$. Substituting $[\gamma u]=-\phi$ from [F1] cancels these terms, leaving $\langle[q],v|_\Gamma\rangle_{\rm bil}=0$. Traces of smooth ambient tests are dense in $H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$ by the chart lift/approximation construction in [F1], so $[q]=0$ in $H^{-1/2}$. [F1, given, algebra]
cases.evidence: Zero density produces zero potentials and all four jumps vanish by linearity.

Let $d,L,N,h,\eta_\varepsilon,Z_{\varepsilon,h}$, and $w_j^{\varepsilon,h}$ have the meanings in [[def-periodic-pic-grid-and-inner-product]] and [[def-periodic-pic-shape-assignment-and-gather]]. For a finite signed Borel measure $\mu$ on the torus, write $\|\mu\|_{\rm TV}=|\mu|(\mathbb T_L^d)$ and define
$$ (P_h^\varepsilon\mu)_j=h^{-d}\int_{\mathbb T_L^d}w_j^{\varepsilon,h}(x)\,d\mu(x). $$ Put $$ C_\eta=\frac{L^d}{12}\sum_{a=1}^d\|\partial_{aa}\eta_\varepsilon\|_\infty,\qquad Z_{\min}=L^d\min_{x\in\mathbb T_L^d}\eta_\varepsilon(x)>0 . $$ Then $\sum_jw_j^{\varepsilon,h}(x)=1$ for every $x$, and $Z_{\varepsilon,h}(x)\ge Z_{\min}$. The measure assignment satisfies $$ \left|(P_h^\varepsilon\mu)_j-(\eta_\varepsilon*\mu)(x_j)\right| \le \frac{C_\eta\|\eta_\varepsilon\|_\infty}{Z_{\min}}\|\mu\|_{\rm TV}h^2 . $$ For $g\in C^2(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb R^m)$ with finite $m\ge1$ (including scalar $m=1$), use the Euclidean norm $|\cdot|_2$ and $\|g\|_\infty=\sup_y|g(y)|_2$. Define the translation-uniform constant
$$ C_{\eta,g}=\frac{L^d}{12}\sum_{a=1}^d \sup_{x,y\in\mathbb T_L^d}\left|\partial_{y_a y_a}\bigl[\eta_\varepsilon(y-x)g(y)\bigr]\right|_2 . $$ The gathered nodal samples satisfy the explicit bound $$ \left|\sum_jw_j^{\varepsilon,h}(x)g(x_j)-(\eta_\varepsilon*g)(x)\right| \le \frac{C_{\eta,g}+C_\eta\|g\|_\infty}{Z_{\min}}h^2 \qquad(x\in\mathbb T_L^d). $$

1.1 Strict positivity of $\eta_\varepsilon$ implies $Z_{\varepsilon,h}(x)>0$. Summing the weights in [F2] gives $\sum_jw_j^{\varepsilon,h}(x)=Z_{\varepsilon,h}(x)/Z_{\varepsilon,h}(x)=1$, and each weight is nonnegative. Since every summand in $Z$ is at least $h^d\min\eta_\varepsilon$, and $h^d|J_N|=L^d$, $Z_{\varepsilon,h}(x)\ge Z_{\min}$. [F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 For fixed $x$, put $f_x(y)=\eta_\varepsilon(y-x)g(y)$ and let $q_x=h^d\sum_jf_x(x_j)-\int f_x(y)\,dy\in\mathbb R^m$. For every Euclidean unit vector $v$, apply the scalar estimate [F3] to $v\cdot f_x$. Since $|v\cdot\partial_{aa}f_x|\le|\partial_{aa}f_x|_2$, this gives $|v\cdot q_x|\le C_{\eta,g}h^2$. If $q_x\ne0$, take $v=q_x/|q_x|_2$; if $q_x=0$ the bound is immediate. Thus $|q_x|_2\le C_{\eta,g}h^2$, with no dimension factor. The integral is $(\eta_\varepsilon*g)(x)$ because the kernel is even. Projecting that integral onto its unit direction in the same way, nonnegativity and the unit integral [F4] give $|(\eta_\varepsilon*g)(x)|_2\le\|g\|_\infty$. The defining supremum is over both $x$ and $y$: translation of the kernel alone does not translate $g$. [F1, F3, F4, algebra]

## Statement

For every real zero-mean source $s$ on the grid of [[def-periodic-pic-grid-and-inner-product]], [[alg-periodic-pic-zero-mean-poisson-solver]] terminates and returns the unique $\phi$ satisfying $A_h\phi=s$ and $\bar\phi=0$. Its incompatible-source branch is taken exactly when the equation has no solution.

1.1 The source and grid contain finitely many real numbers, so computing its mean and finite Fourier transform terminates. If $\bar s\ne0$, then the constant Fourier coefficient of $s$ is nonzero while $A_h$ annihilates constants and has zero constant coefficient on every output, so $A_h\phi=s$ is impossible. [F1, F2, algebra]

## Statement

For every real zero-mean source $s$ on the grid of [[def-periodic-pic-grid-and-inner-product]], [[alg-periodic-pic-zero-mean-poisson-solver]] terminates and returns the unique $\phi$ satisfying $A_h\phi=s$ and $\bar\phi=0$. Its incompatible-source branch is taken exactly when the equation has no solution.

2.1 If $\bar s=0$, its zero Fourier coefficient is zero. By [F1], every other eigenvalue is positive, so all divisions in [F2] are defined. For real input, $\widehat s_{-k}=\overline{\widehat s_k}$ and $\lambda_h(-k)=\lambda_h(k)$; therefore the returned coefficients have the same conjugate symmetry, and pairing the $k$ and $-k$ terms in the inverse transform shows every $\phi_j$ is real. For every nonzero mode, the returned coefficient satisfies $\lambda_h(k)\widehat\phi_k=\widehat s_k$, and the zero mode satisfies $0=\widehat s_0$. Inverse Fourier transformation therefore gives $A_h\phi=s$ and $\widehat\phi_0=0$ gives $\bar\phi=0$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]
cases.evidence: The constant zero eigenvalue is removed before division, while all retained nonconstant eigenvalues are positive.

## Statement

Suppose the step of [[alg-ale-upwind-finite-volume-step]] succeeds and, for every cell,

$$\frac{\Delta t}{\Delta\xi}\left((c_{i+1/2}^n)^+-(c_{i-1/2}^n)^-\right)\le J_i^n.$$

Then the update is monotone, maps nonnegative cell averages to nonnegative cell averages, and for any two input arrays $U,V$ with outputs $U',V'$ it satisfies

$$\sum_iJ_i^{n+1}|U_i'-V_i'|\le\sum_iJ_i^n|U_i-V_i|.$$

1.1 Put $\mu=\Delta t/\Delta\xi$. Expanding the flux difference in [F2] gives $J_i^{n+1}U_i'=\mu(c_{i-1/2}^n)^+U_{i-1}+[J_i^n-\mu((c_{i+1/2}^n)^+-(c_{i-1/2}^n)^-)]U_i-\mu(c_{i+1/2}^n)^-U_{i+1}$. The first and third coefficients are nonnegative by the sign definitions of positive and negative parts; the middle coefficient is nonnegative by the CFL condition. [given, F1, F2, algebra]
cases.reason: The successful ALE step requires positive old and new cell volumes on an actual periodic grid.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathcal T$ be any finite matching shape-regular affine triangulation of a bounded polygonal open set $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^2$, with shape bound $\gamma$ and arbitrary degrees $p_K\ge1$. Set $p_E=\min(p_K,p_{K'})$ on an interior edge, $p_E=p_K$ on a boundary edge, and $m_K=\min_{E\subset\partial K}p_E$. Thus the effective degree retains neighboring shared-trace restrictions, without a bound on degree ratios.

Choose $\chi=1$ and $V=H^1(\Omega)$, or $\chi=0$ and $V=H_0^1(\Omega)$, with Hilbert norm
$$\|v\|_V^2=|v|_{H^1(\Omega)}^2+\chi\|v\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2.$$
Let $V_{\mathcal T,p}$ be the corresponding conforming hp space, imposing zero boundary traces in the $\chi=0$ branch. Suppose the real bilinear form $a$ and real linear functional $F$ satisfy
